extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidance for evaluating whether a claimed species/subgenus is obvious in view of a prior-art genus, including the specific fact-finding and considerations examiners must make under Graham and KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting equivalents known for the same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalents known in the prior art for the same purpose can support an obviousness finding (e.g., GABA-a agonists and ARBs known for alleviating hypertension can motivate combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equivalency must be recognized in the prior art (In re Ruff; Smith v. Hayashi). Applicant's disclosure or mere functional equivalence is insufficient. Use prior-art recognition of equivalence to justify substituting one component/process for another in an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express suggestion to substitute not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: An express suggestion to substitute one equivalent component/process for another is not required to render such substitution obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent an explicit teaching to substitute, substitution may be obvious based on the totality of prior art (In re Fout). Examiners may rely on implicit motivation/suggestion in the art, not only explicit instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-recognized suitability for intended purpose supports obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of a known material based on its suitability for its intended use can support a prima facie obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: choice of a solvent with particular vapor pressure characteristics for printing ink (Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp.). When prior art teaches desired properties and a separate reference teaches specific materials having those properties, combining those teachings may render a claim obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus disclosure alone is insufficient to establish obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that a claimed species/subgenus is encompassed by a prior-art genus does not, by itself, establish a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply per se rules; analyze the facts of each case (In re Baird; In re Papesch; In re Jones). Consider totality of circumstances rather than mechanically treating genus disclosure as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors to establish a prima facie case of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To make out a case of obviousness, examiners must apply the Supreme Court's Graham factors: (A) scope and content of the prior art; (B) differences between the prior art and the claims; (C) level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluation of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie case is made, burden shifts to applicant to rebut. Use the Graham framework to organize fact-finding and ensure a rationale (see KSR). See In re Bell, Rijckaert, Oetiker for burden and analysis discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior art is a genus, make findings on structure, properties, predictability, and number of species
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior-art genus, examiners should find: (A) the structure of the disclosed genus and any expressly described species; (B) any physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed and limitations/problems; (C) predictability of the technology; (D) number of species encompassed, considering all variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These findings help determine whether the genus teaches or suggests the claimed species; document specifics about disclosed species and claimed species comparisons when relying on a genus reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior-art species and the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the closest disclosed species/subgenus in the prior art and explicitly compare similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities to the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The obviousness inquiry focuses on whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex). Document why the chosen prior-art species is the closest and what the relevant differences are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate prior art from the viewpoint of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the relevant time; in many cases the prior art itself supplies the necessary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve the level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity (Ryko; Uniroyal). Consider applicant-submitted evidence if present, and refer to MPEP §§ 2141, 2141.03 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether one of ordinary skill would have had a reason to select the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: After evaluating the Graham factors, determine whether there was a motivation or reason for a skilled artisan to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the key issue in genus-species cases—document teachings or suggestions in the prior art that would have motivated selection and explain how they lead to a prima facie case (Kulling; Panduit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the size of the genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the number and nature of members in the prior-art genus; size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection but a very small, restricted genus may anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small genus with limited variations and a fixed structural nucleus may be tantamount to an explicit disclosure of species (In re Petering; In re Schaumann). Conversely, a large/diffuse genus militates against a per se obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider express teachings in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art expressly teaches selecting or coadministering certain components (e.g., names examples), point to that teaching as a reason to select the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express disclosure or cross-reference to other references can provide motivation to combine or select (Merck & Co. v. Biocraft; In re Kemps). Cite specific statements in the reference that suggest the claimed selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of structural similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the prior art discloses a 'typical', 'preferred', or 'optimum' species structurally similar to the claimed species, which may provide a reason to select the claimed species based on expectation of similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural similarity (homologs, analogs, stereoisomers) often suggests selection (Dillon; Deuel). Consider number and significance of variables to be changed, conservative substitutions in proteins, and whether prior-art preferred species teach toward or away from the claimed species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of similar properties or uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare properties/utilities of structurally similar prior-art species to the claimed species; shared useful properties generally motivate selection, while lack of utility weighs against motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that prior-art species and claimed species share utilities supports a prima facie case (Dillon; Stemniski). If prior art compounds lack utility for the intended purpose, a motivation to make related compounds may be absent (In re Albrecht).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the predictability of the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the relevant technology is predictable; unpredictability reduces the weight of structural similarity in finding obviousness because similar structure may not yield similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts, reasonable expectation of success may be lacking (In re May; In re Schechter). Obviousness requires a reasonable expectation of success, not absolute predictability (In re O’Farrell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider any other relevant teaching (totality of the evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond enumerated categories, consider all relevant prior-art teachings that might support selection of the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed categories (size, express teachings, structural similarity, properties, predictability) are common but not exhaustive—document any unusual or additional teachings that bear on motivation or suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make express fact-findings and provide a KSR-consistent rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make explicit fact-findings on the Graham factors and articulate a rationale (as required by KSR) explaining why the prior art would have motivated selection of the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-findings should state the teachings/suggestions relied on and evaluate whether, taken together, they establish a prima facie case of obviousness. If prima facie established, address applicant rebuttal evidence per MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close structural similarity can create a prima facie case (homologs, isomers, analogs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities—there is an expectation that similar structure implies similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Payne; In re Papesch; In re Dillon) supports obviousness rejections based on structural/functional similarity; ensure utilities align and document the expectation of similar properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology and isomerism must be considered with all other relevant facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Position isomers, homologs, and stereoisomers often give rise to a presumption that similar structure implies similar properties, but this must be weighed with all other facts in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate homology/isomerism automatically with obviousness; consider gaps between homologs/isomers and other contextual facts (In re Wilder; In re Mills; In re Langer).

rubrics_metrics.name: True homologous or isomeric relationship is not controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art need not be a true homolog or isomer to render a claimed compound prima facie obvious; non-homologous but closely similar structures can suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (In re Payne; In re Mayne; In re Merck; In re Dillon) show that structural and property similarity—rather than formal homolog/isomer labels—can support obviousness. Conversely, biological/genetic analogies may differ (In re Bell; In re Deuel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of a prior-art method for making the claimed compound is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the prior art discloses or makes obvious a method of making the claimed compound can affect the obviousness analysis for product claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a known or obvious method for making the compound at the relevant time may rebut a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity (In re Maloney; In re Hoeksema). Consider whether methodology taught in the prior art would have enabled making the claimed compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity is overcome if no reasonable expectation of similar properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption that structural similarity renders a species obvious is rebutted where there is no reasonable expectation that the prior-art structures would share the claimed properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document evidence showing unpredictability or lack of expectation of similar properties; without reasonable expectation of success, structural similarity alone will not sustain a prima facie obviousness rejection.
